'''''Syzygium ingens''''', commonly known as '''red apple''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Peter G. |title=''Acmena ingens'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acmena~ingens |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=22 April 2021}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant that is [[endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is a medium-sized to tall rainforest tree with narrow elliptic to oblong leaves and [[panicle]]s of white flowers on the ends of branchlets, followed by spherical red berries. 

== Description ==
''Syzygium ingens'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of up to {{cvt|40|m}} with a [[Diameter at breast height|dbh]] of up to {{cvt|90|cm}}. It has a smooth, straight, greyish or fawn-coloured trunk that is buttressed at the base of older specimens. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, narrow elliptic to oblong, {{cvt|60–180|mm}} long and {{cvt|20–50|mm}} wide on a reddish [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|2–8|mm}} long. The upper surface of the leaves is glossy green and the lower surface is paler with a raised mid-rib. The flowers are borne in panicles on the ends of branchlets, the panicles shorter than the leaves. The five [[sepal]]s are fused at the base forming a bell-shaped [[Hypanthium|floral cup]] about {{cvt|3|mm}} in diameter with rounded lobes. The five petals are white, more or less oblong and {{cvt|1–2|mm}} long with irregular edges. Flowering occurs from November to December and the fruit is a dark pink to red, spherical to oval [[Berry (botany)|berry]], {{cvt|25–30|mm}} long, {{cvt|15–40|mm}} in diameter containing a single seed surrounded by white flesh.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Floyd">{{cite book |last1=Floyd |first1=Alexander G. |title=Rainforest Trees of Mainland South-eastern Australia |date=1989 |publisher=Inkata Press |isbn=9780958943673 |page=240}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Red apple was first formally described in 1861 by [[Charles Moore (botanist)|Charles Moore]] in ''Catalogue of the Natural and Industrial Products of New South Wales, exhibited in the School of Arts by the International Exhibition Commissioners'' and was given the name ''Nelitris ingens'' from an unpublished description by [[Ferdinand von Mueller]].<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Nelitris ingens''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/492853 |publisher=APNI|access-date=22 April 2021}}</ref> In 1988, [[Gordon P. Guymer]] and [[Bernard Hyland]] changed the name to ''Acmena ingens'' in the journal ''[[Muelleria (journal)|Muelleria]]'',<ref name=APNI2>{{cite web|title=''Acmena ingens''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/485723 |publisher=APNI|access-date=22 April 2021}}</ref><ref name="Guymer">{{cite journal |last1=Guymer |first1=Gordon P. |last2=Hyland |first2=Bernard P.M. |title=A name change in the genus ''Acmena'' DC. (Myrtaceae) |journal=Muelleria |date=1988 |volume=6 |issue=6 |pages=437–438 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/49825859#page/53/mode/1up |access-date=22 April 2021}}</ref> a name that is accepted by the [[National Herbarium of New South Wales]].<ref name="RBGS" />

In 2006, [[Lyndley Craven]] and [[Edward Sturt Biffin]] changed Moore's name ''Nelitris ingens'' to ''Syzygium ingens'' in the journal ''[[Blumea (journal)|Blumea]]'',<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Syzygium ingens''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/611346 |publisher=APNI|access-date=22 April 2021}}</ref><ref name="Blumea">{{cite journal |last1=Craven |first1=Lyndley A. |last2=Biffin |first2=Edward S.A. |last3=Ashton |first3=Peter S. |title=''Acmena'', ''Acmenosperma'', ''Cleistocalyx'', ''Piliocalyx'' and ''Waterhousea'' formally transferred to ''Syzygium'' (Myrtaceae) |journal=Blumea |date=2006 |volume=51 |issue=1 |page=137 |url=https://archive.org/details/blumea-0006-5196-51-131-142/page/n5/mode/2up |access-date=21 April 2021}}</ref> the name accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]<ref name="APC" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Red apple grows on volcanic soil from near [[Gympie]] in south eastern Queensland to [[Casino, New South Wales|Casino]] in northern New South Wales.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Floyd" />

==Ecology==
Birds seen eating the fruit of this species include [[wompoo fruit dove]], [[green catbird]], [[eastern rosella]], [[pied currawong]] and [[topknot pigeon]].<ref name="Floyd" />

==Use in horticulture==
Germination is assisted by removing the seed from the flesh, and soaking for a day or two to kill any insect larvae. Germination is swift and reliable. Cuttings also strike well.<ref name="Floyd" />
